prose

/prohz/ — rhymes with rose · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Prose is ordinary written or spoken language arranged in sentences and paragraphs, as opposed to the rhythmic lines and verses of poetry.

Her clear prose makes even tax law readable.

Example

The author's clear prose in her essay about climate change made complex science accessible to readers without a background in physics.

Prose is precise here because it emphasizes ordinary written language—sentences and paragraphs—as opposed to poetry or verse. The speaker is praising the straightforward, accessible writing style, which is exactly what prose names.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

writing: Writing is anything set down in words — a poem, a grocery list, a contract all count. Prose is one particular form of writing: language arranged in ordinary sentences and paragraphs rather than in verse lines. All prose is writing, but a sonnet is writing that is not prose.

narrative: A narrative is an account that tells connected events — the chain of what happens, in the order a storyteller reveals it. Prose is a medium, not a chain of events: a narrative can be told in prose or in verse, and prose can carry an essay with no events at all.

language: Language is the whole system of words people use, spoken or written, shaped or not. Prose is one specific use of that system: words deliberately arranged into sentences and paragraphs. Every line of prose is language, but language also covers speech, slang, and song.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

poetry: language in rhythmic, image-rich verse form

verse: writing arranged in metered, rhythmic lines

Where it sits · how shaped and musical the language is

speech → verse → prose → poetry

speech vs. prose: Speech is less shaped than prose: speech is language simply spoken aloud, while prose is language deliberately arranged into polished sentences and paragraphs.

verse vs. prose: Verse is more musical than prose: prose flows in ordinary sentences, while verse breaks language into rhythmic, measured lines.

poetry vs. prose: Poetry sits at the far end of the scale from prose: prose aims for clear, direct expression, while poetry compresses language into its most rhythmic, image-rich form.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — prosa (from Old Latin provorsus: pro- 'forward' + vorsus 'turned'): straightforward, moving straight ahead (Latin)

Put it together: Latin prosa (oratio) meant 'straightforward speech' — language that moves straight ahead in plain sentences instead of turning into the rhythmic lines of verse. That is exactly what prose is: ordinary written or spoken language, as opposed to poetry.

Use the root in a new word: prosaic: Prose goes back to Latin prosa — 'moving straight ahead.' Prose walks forward in ordinary sentences instead of turning at the end of every verse, the way poetry does. Call something prosaic and you are calling it that kind of writing: straightforward and everyday, like a recipe or an instruction manual.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Prose is the technical term for ordinary written language arranged in sentences and paragraphs. When you want to distinguish ordinary language from poetry or verse, use prose. For everyday writing, 'writing' or 'text' works fine.
